conflicts.fact: Group number of the noble gases
conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 labels noble gases as Group 0; Lessons 5 and 8 label them Group 18.
Lesson 2 says Group 7; Lesson 8 says Group 17.

conflicts.fact: Sequence order of lessons / what students have already studied
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 covers Group 2 (magnesium and steam), Lesson 4 covers Group 1 and bridges to Group 2 as new content (sets up Lesson 5), and Lesson 6 repeats Group 2 magnesium as if it were new. Lesson 3 says it prepares for halogens in Lesson 4, but Lesson 4 is alkali metals. Lesson 4 draws on electron arrangement from 'Lesson 3', and Lesson 5 says halogens were studied in Lessons 2-4, yet no halogen lesson exists.

conflicts.fact: Where halogens are taught / sodium reaction evidence referenced
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 refers to chlorine bleaching a flower, and Lesson 8 refers to bleaching in Lesson 7 (a Lesson 7 sticky note about bleaching), but Lesson 7 is about transition metals and has no bleaching or halogen investigation; Lesson 8 says the 'elements that do NOTHING' question was posted in Lesson 7, while Lesson 5 covers noble gases.

Lesson 5 research table lists neon with 8 outer electrons while saying all noble gases have full shells (helium 2); Lesson 5 says argon has 'eight outer electrons'; Lesson 8 says helium has two. Lesson 5's DQB says the noble gas question was posted in Lesson 4, while Lesson 8 says it was posted in Lesson 7.

conflicts.fact: Reaction of magnesium with cold water and with steam
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 says magnesium did not react noticeably with cold water and reacted with steam more slowly than with acid; Lesson 6 says in cold water it gave slow tiny bubbles and a Mg(OH)2 film, and steam reaction was 'moderate'. Also Lesson 3 uses 0.5 M HCl, Lesson 6 uses 1 mol/L; Lesson 3 says students test with lit splint, Lesson 6 says teacher only.

conflicts.fact: Why Group 2 is less reactive than Group 1
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 says removing two electrons takes more energy than one; Lesson 6 says the nucleus attracts two outer electrons more effectively than Na's single electron (ignoring that Mg's electrons are lost simultaneously) — framing differs; Lesson 4 attributes reactivity to distance/shielding.

conflicts.fact: Role of sodium electron in lamp glow vs chemical reactivity
conflicts.versions: Lesson 4 says the lamp sodium is 'not reacting chemically' and emits light via electron excitation; Lesson 5 says sodium 'loses its single outer electron to produce the orange glow'; Lesson 6 says the violent reaction with water leads to the orange glow; Lesson 8 says excitation then return to ground state.

conflicts.fact: Calcium hypochlorite tablet behaviour and chlorine as element
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 says the tablet fizzes in water with sharp smell; Lesson 8 explains it via Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO, treating chlorine element reaction, while the phenomenon substance is calcium hypochlorite (a compound).

conflicts.fact: Number of lessons/ DQB question and driving question wording of what is studied
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 says the unit runs eight lessons and model revisited at end of Lesson 7; Lesson 8 is the final model/explanation. Lesson 4 says 80-minute lesson in two 40-min periods while others appear single sessions.

conflicts.fact: Transition metal reaction with dilute acid / cold water
conflicts.versions: Lesson 7 states copper does not react with dilute HCl and iron and zinc react slowly; Lesson 8 says transition metals corrode slowly with no mention; Lesson 7 says zinc protects iron; minor. Also Lesson 8 says copper-based 'noble metals' more inert.
